Continue the previous problem by constructing on the space \(( (0,1], \mathscr{B}((0,1]), \mathrm{P}) \):

(a) a countable system of independent and identically distributed Bernoulli random variables \(\left\{\xi_{n}\right\}_{n \geqslant 1}\) such that

$$
\mathrm{P}\left(\xi_{1}=0\right)=\mathrm{P}\left(\xi_{1}=1\right)=\frac{1}{2}
$$

(b) a sequence of independent random variables \(\left\{U_{n}\right\}_{n \geqslant 1}\) with uniform distribution on \([0,1]\);

(c) a sequence of independent random variables \(\left\{X_{n}\right\}_{n \geqslant 1}\) with given distribution functions \(\left\{F_{n}\right\}_{n \geqslant 1}\);

(d) a sequence of random variables \(\left\{X_{n}\right\}_{n \geqslant 1}\) with given joint distribution functions

$$
\mathrm{P}\left(X_{1} \leqslant x_{1}, \ldots, X_{n} \leqslant x_{n}\right)=F_{n}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right), \quad n \geqslant 1
$$

satisfying the condition

$$
F_{n}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n-1}, \infty\right)=F_{n-1}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n-1}\right)
$$

Establish that on \(([0,1], \mathscr{B}[0,1], \mathrm{P})\), it is impossible to define more than a countable number of independent Bernoulli random variables \(\left\{\xi_{t}\right\}_{t \in T}\) taking two values 0 and 1 with non-zero probability.
reference: \text{It is impossible to define an uncountable number of independent Bernoulli random variables on } ([0,1], \mathscr{B}[0,1], \mathrm{P}).
